the glutathione and the glutathione Stransferase activity show diurnally oscillating rhythms, which are in phase and in opposite phase with the protein content of the liver, respectively.

the circadian rhythms in the concentration of glutathione in the liver of rats and its glutathione S- transferase activity, are inversely related to the circadian rhythm in the level of hepatic protein, and are maximal during the light and minimal during the dark periods of a 24 h light-dark cycle.
the hepatic concentration of glutathione, as well as the glutathione S transferase activity, shows diurnal variations in the rat, with a maximum during daylight and a minimum at dark.

the circadian rhythms in the glutathione and the glutathione S transferase activity of the rat liver.
the circadian rhythms in liver function and their possible implications in toxicology.
the study of the circadian rhythms in the glutathione and the glutathione S- transferase activity in the rat liver.

circadian rhythms in the glutathione level and glutathione transferase activity are present in the liver of rats, but the mechanisms underlying these rhythms are not clear.
the circadian rhythm of glutathione and its S-transferase activity may be an important factor to be considered in toxicological studies.

circadian rhythms in liver glutathione concentration are due to changes in the rate of its synthesis and/or breakdown and are not related to circadian changes in the rate at which the protein content of the liver is synthesized or degraded.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the circadian rhythms in the hepatic levels of glutathione and its conjugating enzyme, glutathione-S-transferase activity, are controlled by a complex interaction of the circadian clock and the fasting clock.
the diurnal variations in glutathione S- transferase activity are related to diurnal variations in the glutathione concentration.
the circadian rhythm is a biological clock, which is synchronized by the environmental factors, such as light and food.

the circadian clock regulates the expression of genes involved in detoxification, and this may be a major factor contributing to the observed diurnal variation in the susceptibility of animals and humans to xenobiotic agents.
circadian rhythms in hepatic glutathione levels may be an important factor that should be considered when studying the toxicity of xenobiotics.
